title: Agent Development with LangChain and LangGraph
objective: Frame the deck around runtime, state, and database responsibilities in production agent systems.
learnerQuestion: What is this deck about?
coreClaim: Production agent development is about model/tool orchestration plus durable state, control flow, and database-backed reliability.
mechanism: LangChain provides high-level agent composition while LangGraph models stateful orchestration and persistence.
example: A support agent answers a ticket, calls tools, pauses for approval, and resumes from checkpointed state.
counterpoint: A demo prompt can appear useful without any durable runtime or database design.
sourceTreatment: Primary docs establish the agent and graph concepts; deck synthesizes them into production design guidance.
practicalTakeaway: Evaluate agent frameworks by runtime responsibilities, not only model prompts.

title: Agents are software systems, not just prompts
objective: Shift the learner from prompt-centric thinking to system design.
learnerQuestion: Why is an agent more than a prompt?
coreClaim: An agent combines model calls, tools, state, permissions, side effects, observability, and product behavior.
mechanism: The model loop depends on surrounding software to expose tools, manage context, enforce policy, and recover from failure.
example: A refund assistant needs tool schemas, auth checks, approval paths, and audit records in addition to a system prompt.
counterpoint: For a one-off exploration, a prompt-only prototype may be sufficient.
sourceTreatment: Official docs describe agents, human review, and observability components that support this systems framing.
practicalTakeaway: Design the control and data plane before trusting an agent with real operations.

title: What you should be able to do after this
objective: Set learning goals around framework choice and database responsibility boundaries.
learnerQuestion: What should I be able to decide after the deck?
coreClaim: A builder should be able to choose LangChain versus LangGraph, map execution state, and assign database responsibilities deliberately.
mechanism: The deck separates agent harness concerns from orchestration and persistence concerns.
example: Choosing a checkpoint store separately from the application database and vector index.
counterpoint: Some teams delegate these boundaries to a hosted platform, but still need to understand them operationally.
sourceTreatment: Source docs define the concepts; the learning goals translate them into practitioner decisions.
practicalTakeaway: Use the deck as a checklist for agent runtime and data architecture.

title: The agent loop
objective: Explain the basic runtime loop behind tool-using agents.
learnerQuestion: What actually happens when an agent runs?
coreClaim: A tool-using agent repeatedly plans, calls tools, observes results, updates context, and decides whether to continue.
mechanism: LangChain's agent APIs build around model/tool interaction loops and stopping conditions.
example: The model requests an order lookup, receives the result, and then drafts an answer.
counterpoint: Not every workload needs an open-ended loop; many are better represented as explicit workflows.
sourceTreatment: Primary docs support the loop and tool-call framing.
practicalTakeaway: Treat the loop as a runtime pattern that needs boundaries, not as magic.

title: LangChain and LangGraph solve different levels
objective: Differentiate the high-level harness from the graph runtime.
learnerQuestion: How do LangChain and LangGraph relate?
coreClaim: LangChain provides standard agent composition while LangGraph provides explicit stateful orchestration.
mechanism: LangChain simplifies model, tool, prompt, and middleware concerns; LangGraph makes nodes, edges, state, persistence, and control flow explicit.
example: Use LangChain to bind tools quickly; use LangGraph to model approval, retry, and resume phases.
counterpoint: LangChain agents can be backed by graph concepts, so this is a level-of-control distinction rather than a hard product boundary.
sourceTreatment: Official docs establish both APIs and their relationship to agent graphs.
practicalTakeaway: Pick the level that matches how much control the product needs.

title: LangChain agents provide the harness
objective: Show why developers start with LangChain.
learnerQuestion: What does LangChain give me right away?
coreClaim: LangChain reduces startup friction by standardizing model, message, tool, middleware, output, and invocation patterns.
mechanism: A single agent construction API can compose tools and model behavior without each team writing its own loop.
example: Bind a lookup function to a model and invoke it through the agent interface.
counterpoint: The harness can hide control-flow details until production requirements force them into view.
sourceTreatment: Primary API docs support the harness description.
practicalTakeaway: Use LangChain to move quickly when the runtime path is still simple.

title: A small agent has a lot around the model
objective: Make the minimal code example concrete.
learnerQuestion: What does a minimal agent invocation include?
coreClaim: Even a compact LangChain example involves model identity, tool definitions, prompts, checkpointing, invocation payloads, and thread identity.
mechanism: The checkpointer and `thread_id` provide durable context boundaries separate from the prompt.
example: `create_agent(...)` with a `lookup_order` tool and an `InMemorySaver` checkpointer.
counterpoint: In-memory checkpointing is appropriate for learning or local development, not production durability.
sourceTreatment: Docs support agent creation and persistence concepts; the code is illustrative.
practicalTakeaway: Keep thread identity and persistence explicit even in small examples.

title: What LangChain hides until you need to care
objective: Expose hidden operational concerns behind simple agent APIs.
learnerQuestion: What can go wrong behind a simple agent call?
coreClaim: Tool schemas, context boundaries, and middleware become operationally important as agents touch real systems.
mechanism: Schemas shape model-callable actions, context carries per-run facts, and middleware centralizes retries, guardrails, summarization, approval, and routing.
example: A tenant id should be context or middleware-controlled, not casually embedded in chat messages.
counterpoint: Small prototypes can defer these concerns until they connect to protected systems.
sourceTreatment: Source docs support tool and review concepts; deck adds failure-mode mapping.
practicalTakeaway: Audit what the harness hides before scaling a prototype.

title: The workflow is mostly an agent loop
objective: Identify when a loop is enough.
learnerQuestion: When is a high-level agent loop acceptable?
coreClaim: A simple loop works when the product mainly needs flexible tool use and response generation without strict phase boundaries.
mechanism: The agent can repeatedly invoke tools until it has enough information or reaches a stopping condition.
example: A read-only support answer bot that looks up orders and summarizes status.
counterpoint: Approval, recovery, and multi-step external effects usually need explicit workflow state.
sourceTreatment: Primary docs support loop behavior; deck adds decision guidance.
practicalTakeaway: Use the loop for flexible reasoning; model workflow phases when correctness depends on them.

title: LangGraph is the orchestration runtime
objective: Define LangGraph's runtime responsibilities.
learnerQuestion: What does LangGraph add?
coreClaim: LangGraph makes state, control, and durability explicit so workflows can be inspected, resumed, and governed.
mechanism: Nodes update typed state, edges route execution, and checkpoints preserve progress.
example: A graph can classify a ticket, draft a response, pause for approval, and resume after a human decision.
counterpoint: Graph modeling adds design overhead for simple conversational agents.
sourceTreatment: Official docs support stateful graph and durable execution framing.
practicalTakeaway: Reach for LangGraph when the control plane is part of the product.

title: A graph is a state machine with execution boundaries
objective: Connect graph design to state-machine thinking.
learnerQuestion: How should I think about graph structure?
coreClaim: A LangGraph workflow is best understood as state moving through explicit execution boundaries.
mechanism: Each node reads state, returns updates, and control flow decides the next node or terminal condition.
example: Classify, retrieve, draft, approve, and execute can be separate graph nodes.
counterpoint: Over-splitting tiny operations can create unnecessary graph noise.
sourceTreatment: Source docs support state-machine and graph workflow design.
practicalTakeaway: Name graph nodes after meaningful product or operational phases.

title: Make phases explicit when phases matter
objective: Show a concrete graph-building example.
learnerQuestion: What does explicit graph code look like?
coreClaim: Typed state and named nodes make workflow phases visible in code.
mechanism: `StateGraph` defines the state shape, nodes, edges, and terminal flow.
example: A ticket workflow classifies risk and drafts a reply as separate nodes.
counterpoint: This simple example omits real retrieval, approval, and error handling.
sourceTreatment: Official docs support graph construction concepts; the example is illustrative.
practicalTakeaway: Use graph code to make important runtime decisions reviewable.

title: Granularity is an operations decision
objective: Teach how to size nodes and phases.
learnerQuestion: How granular should a graph be?
coreClaim: Node granularity should follow retry, observability, approval, and recovery boundaries.
mechanism: A node boundary becomes a useful place to inspect state, checkpoint progress, branch, or resume.
example: Put an external write in its own node if it needs idempotency and audit handling.
counterpoint: Very fine-grained graphs can be harder to understand and maintain.
sourceTreatment: Docs support graph design, durability, and trace concepts; deck synthesizes operational sizing guidance.
practicalTakeaway: Draw boundaries where operations need control, not around every helper function.

title: Durability changes failure semantics
objective: Explain durability tradeoffs.
learnerQuestion: What does checkpoint durability change?
coreClaim: Checkpoint timing changes the tradeoff between write overhead and the amount of work that can be lost or repeated after failure.
mechanism: Durable execution uses persistence to save state so runs can resume from known boundaries.
example: A critical approval step may prefer stronger checkpoint guarantees than a read-only lookup.
counterpoint: Stronger checkpointing can add latency or storage overhead.
sourceTreatment: Official docs support durable execution and persistence; the table turns that into decision guidance.
practicalTakeaway: Tune durability to the cost of redo, data loss, and latency.

title: Interrupts turn review into a runtime primitive
objective: Explain human approval as part of execution, not a side channel.
learnerQuestion: How does human review fit into agent runtime?
coreClaim: Interrupts let a graph pause, persist state, wait for external input, and resume with the same thread context.
mechanism: Persistence stores paused graph state and resume commands continue execution after review.
example: A high-risk billing change pauses until a human approves or edits the proposed action.
counterpoint: Review UI, authorization, and audit trails still need to be built by the application.
sourceTreatment: Official docs support interrupts, persistence, and human-in-the-loop concepts.
practicalTakeaway: Treat approval as a persisted workflow state, not a chat message.

title: Databases are not one thing in an agent system
objective: Separate database responsibilities.
learnerQuestion: What database does an agent need?
coreClaim: Production agents usually need multiple data responsibilities rather than one generic agent database.
mechanism: Business truth, execution checkpoints, short-term memory, long-term memory, vector retrieval, queues, audit, and traces optimize for different access patterns.
example: Orders live in the app database, graph state in a checkpoint store, and policies in a retrieval index.
counterpoint: A single physical database can host multiple roles if schemas, access patterns, and guarantees are separated.
sourceTreatment: Sources establish individual data responsibilities; deck synthesizes the responsibility map.
practicalTakeaway: Name each data role before choosing storage technology.

title: The app database remains the source of business truth
objective: Keep domain truth out of agent internals.
learnerQuestion: Where should orders, users, invoices, and permissions live?
coreClaim: Business truth should remain in the application database and be exposed to agents through narrow, authorized tools.
mechanism: Tools can enforce permissions and invariants before reading or writing durable records.
example: A tool checks whether the user may view an invoice before returning invoice data to the model.
counterpoint: An app database may also provide vector or memory features, but the domain boundary still matters.
sourceTreatment: Sources support tool use and side-effect reliability; deck applies standard system design boundaries.
practicalTakeaway: Do not let model context become the system of record.

title: Checkpoint databases store execution state, not domain truth
objective: Clarify checkpoint storage semantics.
learnerQuestion: What belongs in a checkpoint database?
coreClaim: Checkpoint stores persist thread and graph execution state so runs can resume, inspect history, and pause for review.
mechanism: Checkpointers store snapshots and metadata tied to thread or checkpoint identifiers.
example: Use SQLite or memory for local tests and a durable backend for production graph runs.
counterpoint: Checkpoint data may reference domain records, but it should not replace those records.
sourceTreatment: Official docs support checkpointing, persistence, and backend integration claims.
practicalTakeaway: Separate execution recovery from business state management.

title: Short-term memory and long-term memory are different stores
objective: Distinguish memory scopes.
learnerQuestion: What does memory mean in an agent app?
coreClaim: Short-term memory supports thread continuity while long-term memory persists reusable information across sessions, users, or namespaces.
mechanism: Memory policies define keys, retention, correction, deletion, and read/write behavior.
example: A thread summary helps continue a ticket; a user preference memory carries across future tickets.
counterpoint: Bad long-term memory can become persistent product behavior and needs governance.
sourceTreatment: Official memory and persistence docs support the distinction.
practicalTakeaway: Define memory write policy before persisting model-derived facts.

title: Vector search is a context source, not memory by itself
objective: Avoid conflating retrieval with memory.
learnerQuestion: Is a vector database an agent memory?
coreClaim: Vector search retrieves relevant context, but memory is product state the system chooses to carry forward.
mechanism: Embedding indexes make content searchable; retrievers decide ranking, filters, permissions, freshness, and chunk strategy.
example: A policy document retrieved from MongoDB Vector Search or pgvector is evidence for a response, not a memory of the user.
counterpoint: Long-term memory can be implemented with vector search, but only with explicit write, scope, and deletion policies.
sourceTreatment: Sources establish vector retrieval and memory concepts; deck distinguishes their semantics.
practicalTakeaway: Use retrieval for evidence; use governed memory for persistent personalization.

title: Use queues and outboxes for reliable action
objective: Connect agent side effects to distributed-systems reliability patterns.
learnerQuestion: How should agents perform durable side effects?
coreClaim: Agent-triggered side effects should be recorded and processed idempotently because loops, retries, pauses, and external APIs can fail independently.
mechanism: A transactional outbox records intended effects with the domain transaction, then processors deliver them reliably.
example: Record a refund request intent before an asynchronous worker calls a payment provider.
counterpoint: Read-only tools may not need an outbox, but they still need auth and observability.
sourceTreatment: AWS guidance supports outbox pattern; LangGraph docs support long-running/retry context.
practicalTakeaway: Design tools so retrying them cannot corrupt state.

title: Traces explain behavior better than logs alone
objective: Show why agent observability needs structured traces.
learnerQuestion: Why are logs not enough?
coreClaim: Agent behavior spans model calls, tool calls, retrievers, parsers, nodes, metadata, and feedback, so traces give a more useful debugging surface than flat logs.
mechanism: A trace connects runs and metadata for one user operation or agent turn.
example: A bad answer can be debugged by inspecting retrieved chunks, model input, tool output, and node path.
counterpoint: Traditional logs are still useful for infrastructure health and error reporting.
sourceTreatment: Official LangSmith docs support trace/run/metadata/feedback concepts.
practicalTakeaway: Instrument agents around decisions and dependencies, not just exceptions.

title: A pragmatic architecture
objective: Assemble the parts into a production architecture.
learnerQuestion: What does a practical agent architecture include?
coreClaim: A production agent architecture combines an agent runtime, graph checkpointing, business tools, retrieval, memory, reliable side effects, audit, and observability.
mechanism: Each component owns a different operational responsibility and data lifecycle.
example: A support agent uses LangGraph for state, MongoDB/Postgres for domain data, vector search for KB retrieval, an outbox for side effects, and traces for debugging.
counterpoint: A smaller app can start with fewer components if the product promises are narrower.
sourceTreatment: Sources establish component capabilities; deck synthesizes architecture guidance.
practicalTakeaway: Build from product guarantees to runtime and data components.

title: Start from product promises
objective: Translate user promises into technical requirements.
learnerQuestion: How do I decide which runtime features I need?
coreClaim: Runtime and database choices should follow product promises such as continue later, approval, learning preferences, and knowledge-base use.
mechanism: Each promise creates concrete requirements around checkpointing, interrupts, memory, retrieval, permissions, and evaluation.
example: A 'come back later' promise requires thread ids, a checkpointer, retention policy, and state inspection.
counterpoint: Overbuilding every feature up front can slow a narrow MVP.
sourceTreatment: Docs support individual mechanisms; deck maps them to product promises.
practicalTakeaway: State the promise before picking the framework knob.

title: Where agent systems usually break
objective: Summarize common failure patterns.
learnerQuestion: What should I watch for in production?
coreClaim: Agent systems usually fail at boundaries: state scope, retrieval quality, side effects, approval handling, permissions, and observability.
mechanism: Each boundary couples model behavior to application infrastructure and distributed-system guarantees.
example: A model retries a tool call after a timeout and accidentally performs a duplicate external action.
counterpoint: Some failures are model quality issues, but many are ordinary software architecture issues.
sourceTreatment: Sources support the underlying mechanisms; deck synthesizes operational failure modes.
practicalTakeaway: Test boundary failures, not only happy-path model responses.

title: LangChain first, LangGraph when control becomes product logic
objective: Give a practical adoption rule.
learnerQuestion: Which framework should I start with?
coreClaim: Start with LangChain when the harness is enough; move to LangGraph when control flow, durability, review, and recovery are product requirements.
mechanism: LangGraph exposes state and graph execution boundaries that high-level agent loops can obscure.
example: A read-only Q&A bot may stay in LangChain; a regulated case-resolution workflow should model phases in LangGraph.
counterpoint: Teams with known workflow complexity can begin with LangGraph from day one.
sourceTreatment: Source docs establish capabilities; deck translates them into an adoption heuristic.
practicalTakeaway: Let product control requirements determine how explicit the runtime should be.

title: The useful mental model
objective: Recap the layered architecture.
learnerQuestion: What should I remember?
coreClaim: Think in layers: LangChain for harness, LangGraph for stateful control, and databases for differentiated persistence responsibilities.
mechanism: Each layer reduces a different class of complexity and failure.
example: Tool invocation belongs in the harness; approval and resume belong in graph state; order data belongs in the app database.
counterpoint: Real systems may collapse layers physically, but logical separation remains useful.
sourceTreatment: Source docs support individual layers; recap synthesizes them.
practicalTakeaway: Do not use one abstraction to solve every agent-system responsibility.

title: Follow-up reading by concept
objective: Provide source paths for continued learning.
learnerQuestion: Where should I go next?
coreClaim: The most useful follow-up reading is grouped by agent harness, graph runtime, persistence and memory, retrieval, reliability, and observability.
mechanism: Each reference supports a specific concept used in the deck.
example: Read LangGraph persistence and checkpointer docs before choosing a production checkpoint backend.
counterpoint: Framework docs change quickly, so examples should be checked against current package versions.
sourceTreatment: References slide points readers to primary sources.
practicalTakeaway: Use primary docs for API specifics and this deck for architecture framing.
